utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We will now resume our work. I understand we also have a new court deputy among us. He will now please call the case number, Mr. Abtahi, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances please, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Goran Mikulicic, and along with Mr. Joka I represent the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that for this week there are two witnesses, as far as the Prosecution is concerned. Mr. Neimann, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, Your Honours, there are two witnesses that the Prosecution wishes to call in rebuttal, and in respect to both of those witnesses, Your Honours, we are seeking some protective measures and we have notified our colleague Mr. Mikulicic of that. The protective orders that we seek in respect of both of them, Your Honours, is that they be referred to by pseudonym rather than their own name, and that the image of their face be distorted when they give their evidence. Other than that, Your Honours, there are no other protective measures that are sought by us, but in relation to that, we do seek that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, is there anything you would like to add, observations you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no comments and no objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Neimann, what is the aim of the Prosecution as far as calling these witnesses is concerned? Are they witnesses of fact or witnesses of character? What are they exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, let me characterise them for you. Both of the witnesses give testimony of a similar nature, so I can speak of them together. The evidence that they will give will touch upon matters that were raised directly by the Defence in the course of their defence case. They will deal with, firstly, the circumstances of the issue of the conflict. There has been suggested by the Defence, in the course of their case, that the conflict initiated was initiated more or less by the Muslim forces as an attack upon the Croatian people who were in the Lasva Valley at the time. These people, who are Muslim witnesses, will give their version of those events, and how they perceived it, and how they saw the issues develop during the latter course of 1992 and early 1993. We will also touch upon the issue of them being arrested for the sake of their protection. It's been suggested that there was some benevolent purpose in them being taken to the Kaonik camp, that purpose being to insure that they were protected from the effects of the war, and perhaps people surrounding them. Their evidence will seek to rebut that, and in fact go to establish the contrary. We will then move on to the position of trench digging. Your Honours have heard evidence that the conditions under which the people were engaged in trench digging was universal, the same, it applied for the Croatian inhabitants of the area and for the Muslim people who were in the Kaonik camp. These witnesses will seek to refute that and show that the situation with respect to them was considerably different than that which Your Honours have heard pertained to the Croatian people. Your Honours, that's generally the course. Both the witnesses were detained in the Kaonik camp and subsequently exchanged; so, that's the effect of that evidence. And that's the only evidence in rebuttal that we seek to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neimann. That's a very complete outline that you've just given us. Now, the bench will grant these witnesses the protective measures that you have asked for and I will turn to the technical booth. Technicians, are we ready? Can we begin with the deposition of these witnesses? Yes, thank you very much. Can the witnesses be brought in, please? Or the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the first witness be referred -- they have the wrong witness, Your Honour. Might the first witness be referred to with pseudonym V, Your Honour. And the gentleman we have just seen is Witness W. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now take the oath, the usher is holding out the text for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. Do you feel comfortable, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now answer the questions put to you by Mr. Neimann, the gentleman on your right. Mr. Neimann, you have the floor

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: WITNESS V Examined by Mr. Niemann:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Their Honours have granted you certain protective measures so you may give your evidence. During the course of your evidence we will refer to you by the name Witness V. Their Honours have also ordered that the image of your face be distorted during the course of your testimony. I now ask you to please look at a piece of paper that I show you, and don't tell me the name that's on it; but would you tell me whether it is your name that you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be shown to the Defence, and I tender that, Your Honour, as a sealed exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness V, during the course of your testimony, please do not refer to your name or give details of matters which may tend to identify you, other than those matters that I directly ask you questions about. Witness V, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do military service when you were living in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did military service, did you receive any specialist training, such as officer training or training of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you completed your military service 20 years ago, did you then have any involvement with the military from that date through until 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a reservist, or did you have any other connection with the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, if there was anything, it was civilian protection, and it was more administrative type of work, planning and such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have some higher education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What level of higher education did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would prefer not to answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you employed from the period after you left military service through until 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of your employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have the same work all that period of time, or did it vary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same type of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you employed? What town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, were you employed for the whole period in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any political affiliations during the period of your adult life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was active in the local commune FDP. Anything that existed in the system of that time. I was not in the leadership, but I did -- I was involved in those activities, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was the period when the Communist Party was in control of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did you become a member of any of the parties, the SDA, the HDZ, or any of those political parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I remained, politically speaking, on the positions which I held before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you tell Their Honours the condition of the relationship that existed between the Muslim people and the Croatian people in the Lasva Valley area, particularly Busovaca, during the period of 1992 through to 1993? What were conditions and relations like between those two peoples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Individually speaking, 1992, and in general, was a crossroads, and it changed the harmonious relationship which existed between the two ethnic groups, which was throughout the region. However, following the elections, the tensions could be felt and people started taking distance from one another. Then there was the HDZ, which tried to out vote us in the local assembly, and then the HVO in May tried to take over a depot of the JNA with shooting, and then they hoisted their flag, which we called the checkerboard and they called the Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stop there. I think perhaps you need to go a little slower, because what you say has to be interpreted and I think you're going a little bit fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's okay. Now, you say in May these events happened, May of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, April or May, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say there was some sort of dispute about the raising of flags; do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did not allow Bosnians to put out any symbols, then there were demonstrations of force. There was shooting, and then, as far as I learned, I did not see this, they had taken, they had transported the weapons from Kaonik to Tisovac, then the takeover and the changing the frequency for the television, local television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll just break it up if we can, and perhaps you might just answer my questions and it might make it easier for us to get through it. Who had control over the local --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had control over the local government administration in Busovaca during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they take control in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a result of them being successful in the elections of that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to enter into politics, but in any event, not only because they won the elections, I believe that they did not have an absolute majority, if that was your question. There was also force which was used there, and also some cheating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at first, when the HDZ came in charge of the local administration, was there an attempt made by both the Muslim and Croat peoples to work together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout this time the population, the Croats, Bosniaks and Serbs tried to create a front and organised an army -- I don't know how to call it -- especially the citizens of Busovaca, which would be mixed in order to resist the aggression. Because the war in Croatia was already raging at that time and different forces were trying to break this up, and the command structure could not established. I think they had three or four meetings in the sports hall. We tried to establish a unit which would defend Busovaca. However, through obstruction and in different ways, both Croats and Serbs and the Bosniaks who were for it were either intimidated or would give up, so that this mixed unit was never established. It never came alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were lists of people's names taken, nonetheless, that would form part of this combined force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that there was a list, the short list of commanders, I believe it existed. I think that somebody was taking notes. I attended these meetings as a regular citizen who was supposed to defend Bosnia, and I don't know whether the organising committee had those lists or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during 1992, '93, were you able to receive television transmissions in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a certain period until May we did. However, after that we could then receive some signal from other transmitters, not from the Skradno transmitter. After that we could locally only receive the programmes in Croatian language. I believe this was Croatian television. You could sense that this was Croatian television. But in order to stay calm, so to speak, I did not follow these programmes very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who controlled the local television transmissions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HDZ, I don't know the individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was being broadcast over the local television that you were able to see when you did watch it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, it was the news from the Croatian front, and then entertainment programmes. And all the language used in the translations, it was incomprehensible, we had not learned those new words yet, so, we were irritated by it. So, we watched it as little as we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any programmes that you, yourself, saw that were directed against Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that in 1992 it would have been a bit early. I believe that this happened only in 1993, but at that time I was no longer in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you didn't see anything in 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know of any fighting that took place between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, during the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of any fighting or conflict that took place between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO during 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1993 I was taken to the camp sometime in late January, and even then I did not believe that there was fighting. However, I was there in camp and the fighting started in the Lasva River Valley, and I did not hear of any other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now who started the fighting in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each side had their own view on this. I still believe that this was the HVO because if you look in a broader context during the attack of the HVO against the units in Busovaca, there were still areas like Zenica where the people could live normally. And, as I learned, the HVO even had an organisation in Zenica. So my view, even though I may not be competent to say this, it was the HVO which started because they were organised, they were armed, they had control over the main communication lines, so they had everything they needed for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now prior to your arrest, did you notice any changes taking place in the Town of Busovaca itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were some changes in the Town of Busovaca throughout 1992, according to the following system: hot/cold, hot/cold. One day it would be good for the Bosniaks; the next day they would be shooting, the Bosniaks would be terrified. Their Croat friends would say these were fools who were shooting, don't pay any attention to it, and that was more or less what all of what '92 was like. Some events perhaps demonstrate that this was done according to a plan. I think that at that point, the flag of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was raised and then orders were given to respond by force, and then shooting started from the hills around the town. Then we in the town were wondering against whom was this directed? We were all looking at each other and wondering. This demonstration of force showed that the target was the town itself, and we thought that the town should defend itself. We realised that the surrounding villages could also be subjected to artillery fire, so this was a true demonstration of force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was firing this artillery on the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody was firing on the town, but they wanted to disperse gatherings where Bosniaks were present and specifically one rally where the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina was raised on the building of the fire brigade and orders were given to demonstrate force. I imagine that they were shooting without any special target, just into the air, but they wanted the Bosniaks to disperse when they would hear the shooting. And there were some 20-odd soldiers there with long rifles around the people who were at this gathering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think they were Croats because they wore camouflage uniforms and at that time Bosniak and Busovaca could not have this camouflage uniform because this could have only been the case if he came from the Croatian front, but he was not allowed to have one or wear one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any of the soldiers that were involved personally from the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did. Perhaps some of the elderly people. I knew my own generation, but the younger people, children in particular, in uniforms, I didn't really recognise them. Although, there were some unknown people who were older too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any unknown soldiers in the town in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the town towards Tisovac, and in that direction I mean, and in various instances, unknown soldiers would appear and there were different uniforms too. It was a parade of sorts of different uniforms, different insignia, however, we moved about very little. So at any rate there were quite a few unknown people whom we did not know. At least in the circle of people that I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people appear to be connected to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was obvious. It was obvious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now were you told or did you hear of what the aims and objectives of the HVO were at that time in January of 1993 in relation to Busovaca and its surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In every day conversations with colleagues and friends, mention was made of the current political situation, what would happen, whether the former Yugoslavia would survive and, in that context. We came to learn quite a few things from what the Croats would tell too, some of them were more informed, others were less informed. But they were saying that Croatia would be there and that perhaps even Zenica would belong to Croatia. Perhaps Zenica would be part of Croatia too. All of this was told in a way which implied that there would be a division, a partition, because they said that the Serbs would kill all Muslims, so the Muslims should come with the Croats. There were quite a few stories to that effect, that that would be Croatia, and that people already felt a certain trend to this effect. The new Croatian language was being emphasised. The Croatian Dinar was introduced in the meantime too; the BH Dinar was suppressed. Food and cigarettes and other consumer goods could only be bought for Croatian Dinars or German Marks, according to an exchange rate that was dictated by the HVO because it was only the HVO that allowed the circulation of goods in that territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now in January of 1993, late January of 1993, did anything happen, or were there any incidents concerning the businesses of Muslim people in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well things were happening. There were individual cases of mining shops, blowing up shops, arresting certain people. All of this was in 1992. However, in January 1993, all Bosnian Muslim businesses in Busovaca were bombed and they were all blown up. At that time we didn't even have telephones. I noticed at the time as I communicated with my Croatian friends, neighbours, whatever you choose to call them, that they were afraid, that they were reluctant to communicate, but we never thought that something would happen of the magnitude of the things that did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the Croatian businesses in Busovaca attacked in a similar way that you can recollect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any such instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who had mined or attacked these businesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were in power and who had the money. Bosniaks couldn't pass and certain groups could not move anywhere. There was rigorous control, so we weren't even allowed to leave town. So it was the government, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now what happened to you personally in late January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In late January, 1993, in the evening, three men in uniform knocked at my door. When I opened the door, they said "hello" and they swore at me immediately and they said, give me weapons. I said very calmly, "Young men, I don't have any weapons and you are free to search the house." And they said, "We are not going to search the house at all, but don't open the door to anyone."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who these people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know the men who came that night. Two of them were wearing stockings over their faces and one had his face revealed. He was a youngish man, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether they -- what nationality they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one could have come to my place at that time except a Croat because in that part of the building where I lived at the time I was the only Bosniak left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other apartments occupied by Croatian people in that building or Bosniak Croats in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many apartments were there in the block?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were around 32 apartments and I think that the situation was half/half. Perhaps there were a Bosniak or two more, but, at any rate, it was more or less half/half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now what happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning between six and seven o'clock, three men came to my door. They said there is a war outside, come with us so that we can put you away. I asked whether I should take some of my personal belongings because it was illogical for me to go to a shelter without some water, some food reserve, cigarettes, whatever. He said, never mind, you'll be back soon, so I locked the door of my apartment and I left. He showed me that I should move towards the police station and they hid behind the building. I reached the police station and I wanted to enter the building quite normally. However, people in camouflage uniforms ordered me to board a big transport truck, a lorry, which did not even have a cover on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first met these gentlemen at six or seven in the morning, did you gain the impression that they came to move you from the building for your own protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when they told me that I didn't need any of my things, my own things, then I stopped thinking that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you left the building, started to leave the building itself, did you see any of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the neighbours from different floors of my building were watching this. I cast a glance that way and it seemed to me that they just happened to be watching, but, at any rate, they saw me being taken out of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now these people that were watching you, what was their nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of them gathered up and taken by the police -- or, by the three men in uniform at the same time or was it only you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the truck with me was my neighbour Anto Drazic. When he was told -- when he said at Kaonik that he was a Croat, he was released immediately. I cannot say that he was released for good, but at any rate he was released from my cell, he left my cell after saying that he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that he had been arrested by mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was arrested by mistake because I see no point. I mean, I mean he was a man who was a normal person in that situation. I don't think it was any kind of repression or anything. I simply think it was a mistake not knowing who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of the other people that were arrested at that time, the same time as you, apart from this one man, your neighbour, what was their nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, and I am speaking of the time when I left, there was another Bosniak with me. And, after that, there was a clamour in the camp, shouting, it was Bosniaks who are being brought in en masse. These were the Bosniaks from Busovaca who happened to be at their homes. There weren't any Croats there. I do not know of a single other case, except for the one I told you about, which I think was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you arrived at Kaonik, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me into a cell and I was surprised. These were military hangars. I saw that the purpose of these facilities had been changed. That a classical prison was made out of this place, a camp, whatever you choose to call it. I wondered why this was done, and for whom this was done, during 1992, but we Bosniaks did not know about it, at least I wasn't aware of it. I was surprised, so they took me into a cell and three men came in after me, two of them wore stockings over their faces and one of them had his face revealed and he was cursing my balija mother. He was saying that the BH army had massacred Croats. That they were cutting off their ears, noses, genitals and that he said that, "I am going to do all those same things to you." I was petrified, of course, not believing that something like that could happen, let alone that it would happen to me. He ordered me to take everything out of my pockets. I did that. I put it all in front of me. I had some money amounting to up to 500 Deutschemarks it was all in Croat Dinars, BH Dinars and German Marks, but the equivalent of 500 Deutschemarks. He took these bank notes and he left. The two camouflage men were outside, and after that they came in and they asked me, "Did the other guy take anything from you?" I lied, I said "No." After that, I was so pleased that I did that because I saw cases when a man would say yes, and then he would be beaten up after that. Then they started bringing quite a few people in and this was a room of about 12 square metres all together, to the best of my recollection, and there were about 40 of us in there. There wasn't enough room to stand in there. This entire hangar was full. You could hear people yelling, shouting. Around twelve o'clock they asked who would want to say their noon prayers? The Muslim prayer at noon. And then this was taped by video camera and I heard that this was played on television. That they were even allowed to say their prayers, et cetera. However, throughout my stay in the prison, this was never allowed again. So I think that this was a propaganda matter all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many people were approximately in your cell in or put into your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to lie down or sit down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No way, whoever could sit down would be lucky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept there in this condition with all these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They kept us until they started sending us to dig trenches, and that was the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any toilet facility in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, not in the room. There was a joint toilet out there and there were plain barrels with drinking water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about food, were you given any food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were given a plate full of soup per two or three men, depending on how many could actually fit in and get this food. So that was all the food we received and it wasn't really enough to satisfy your hunger, no. No, and there was no peace. You'd have to eat in haste and it would be too hot and you would have to hurry. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were arrested, did you have a medical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had some stomach trouble, and I was supposed to lead a tranquil life. I wasn't supposed to get nervous or anything. That is probably why I was not involved in other affairs. I had devoted myself to my family and I, therefore, had problems when I got there. My condition got worse and I asked the guards to take me to see a doctor. I asked them twice, and I am not sure whether they asked someone about it or not. At any rate, I didn't go that day. The next day, again I asked to be taken to see the warden. I asked them to let me see the warden. But when I said "warden" when I said the warden, the commander, then the guard understood me. He took me to a man who had a table in the middle of this hangar and he was standing there. I told him about the problems I had and he sort of waved his hands and I interpreted this as meaning no go. I insisted again in the afternoon. Again the same gesture, everything was the same. However, as night fell a guard came and he said, come on. I was escorted by two soldiers and a driver to the medical centre and I found a lady doctor there. I had never seen her before and this was a small town, you know, so we all knew each other personally and I was surprised when I saw that this was a new lady doctor. She hadn't been working there at all before that, so I didn't really expect any assistance. However, then I was given an injection and some tablets and they wrote out certain findings to the effect that I needed treatment at home and I needed to rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lady doctor at the medical centre who was on duty that night. I didn't know her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The note that she wrote it down on, were you given that note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, she gave me these findings. She gave me these findings. She said, well, take this and give it to them over there if it can help you any. It was something to that effect. I cannot exactly interpret all her words, but that is what it was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was so happy, you know, to show this to the driver and these soldiers and I said, I'll be going home. The driver took this paper and he said, well we'll have to see with the warden. In the meantime, we were passing my apartment and I happened to look at the balcony and I saw lights on. Other people on the balcony and I knew that none of the members of my family were there and I saw what the situation was. They brought me back to the camp. They gave the warden this little piece of paper again. He had just waved his hands as was his custom and he turned and walked away. I expected him to do something, to transfer me at least to a cell where I could sit down or lie down, but nothing. In the morning my name was one of the first to be called out from the hallway and they called out a few more people, the names of a few more people. They loaded us on a truck and we were escorted to Groblje in Busovaca and we were ordered to dig graves. That is the Muslim part of the Groblje cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stopping there and going back to the incident with the note, were you present when the note was handed to the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. This is the way he looked at it. Here, the tape, I mean I had to stand 3 metres behind him, but I saw this guy put him it on the table right in front of him and show it to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when it was, can you tell us in more detail what the commander of the camp did when he saw the note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He gestured. I said I was standing 3 metres away from the table. I wanted to hear what would happen, but his gesture and everything showed that he simply ignored these findings. I cannot recall what he exactly said, but I remember the gesture. I remember the way he waved his hands, meaning nothing doing or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the commander then keep the note or did he give it back to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't give it back to me. It remained there, in the camp. It wasn't given back to me, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This commander, did you subsequently come to know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that they called him Zlatko over there, but while I was in the camp I found out that his last name was Aleksovski. All of this was a bit strange to me. How come this man came there? He was not from Busovaca. He was not from Busovaca by origin, so I remember that in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Zlatko Aleksovski that took the note from you, did you see him on more occasions during the time you were in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him when we went out to work, or in passing when we were being taken somewhere. After that day when I was called out I had no further contacts with him, nor would I have asked him for help even if I was dying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that you would be able to recognize that person if you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he did not change physically in the last six years I believe I would be able to recognize him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might look around the courtroom now and see if you can see that person that you were told was Zlatko Aleksovski; and if you can, would you point to him, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this is the gentleman that is sitting next to the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that the witness has identified the accused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look for me, now, at Exhibit 18H. It's a Defence exhibit, 18H Defence exhibit. Would you look for me, please, carefully at this document and tell me whether you recognize it as a copy of any document that you've seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that this is a copy of the document which I gave to the driver of the car, which was then turned over to the warden of the camp. It could have been smaller size, but based on the text, I saw the brand name of the medication, and I recall that I was given those tablets. I was surprised that in addition to the injection I was also given some tablets, and I had been wondering why I had not been released. So I thought maybe it had to do with the Latin words, that who knows what she wrote down. So, this is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could we have it on the projector? And the English version, as well, I think should be shown. Just put that for the moment, and we will follow up with the English version of that. Could the English version be placed now on the screen? Remove the English version now, please. Perhaps it might be shown to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what the symptoms of your medical condition were? Don't be embarrassed about going into detail, but can you tell Your Honours what was happening to you as a consequence of your medical condition at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that psychological problems, I think it was fear. I think that I was psychologically shattered. It was from all the fear from, afraid, nerves, I think that it had its effect. I was upset mentally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the effect, apart from the mental side of it? What was the physical effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see from the finding, I think that you see the description, I would prefer not to repeat it. When I went to relieve myself, I saw what it was, and I knew that I had to seek medical attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were passing bloody stools; were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you said the next day your name was called out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you just called out on your own or were you with a group of other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called out among the first, and later on the rest of the group was called out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many in the group were called?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Neimann, I think maybe this would be a good time to take a break, it would enable the witness to take a break and rest. So it's a 20-minute break for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Neimann, you have the floor. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness V, you were telling us just before the break about an incident where you were called out after the next morning, after you had been to see the doctor, with a group of other people. And I asked you how many people were in that group that were called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten people, somewhere around ten. And later on I confirmed that it was ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your medical condition like on that day when you were called out the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not better. It was a chronic condition. It goes on for days and it is not something that is fixed by a single treatment. It has to do with stabilising both the mental condition and the diet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken? I think you mentioned you were taken to a grave site; where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the cemetery in Busovaca. It's a Muslim Bosniak cemetery, and there we were ordered to dig graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who ordered you to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards who escorted us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told beforehand, or informed before you left the Kaonik facility whether or not, what you were doing, what you were supposed to be doing that day? Did anyone tell you what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, simply we were ordered to enter the vehicle, and without any information we were just taken there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the guard that took you there, was he armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were armed, yes. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were kept under guard, were you, so that you couldn't escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, just precisely what were you ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To select a location that is an unused space in the cemetery, and two men were assigned to each dig a grave. So, five groups of two are digging five graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we dug, we could hear small arms shooting, and we were told by a guard that the Muslim snipers were shooting. However, I concluded that they were trying to intimidate us by shooting the fragmentation bullets. This went on in certain intervals. When we finished, two Bosniaks improvised a cart, I don't know the size, maybe one metre in length. They brought the first two bodies, which were stacked, and the limbs were dangling. When I saw this sight I just felt revulsion, and I could not follow this and I could not watch this anymore; so I just mechanically kept on doing what I had been ordered to do. There was no religious ritual or anything, we simply buried them. It was as if these weren't people. It was extremely humiliating. It was one of the worst scenes which I experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognize any of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was Merdan Nihad. I don't know his real name but I know Merdan Ceri was his nickname, and then it was a man called Novalic, I don't know his first name. Then I believe Irhan, son of Fahrudin Mehmescic. Unfortunately right now I cannot recall the fifth one, I would have to think further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the nationality of these people who were dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Bosniaks. The local inhabitants of Busovaca who had houses there where they had been killed, in that part of town where they were killed, where they were murdered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had any connection with the military, or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is something that the Court may want to judge. I think that maybe formally they were members of the army, but they couldn't do anything. I don't believe that they were on any kind of rebellion or uprising. That would have been insane. The whole place was surrounded by the HVO, so it would have been insane to have attempted anything. But given their age, they could have been members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We buried them as civilians, they were wearing civilian clothes. I said that formerly perhaps they could be, they could have been members of the army; but they were wearing civilian clothes. They looked like people who were not prepared for any of this, because it was January, they did not wear warm winter clothing. They were wearing the lighter clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see how they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given my condition, my mental state, I told myself I could not bear to face this and I did not watch. I saw blood, I saw that, but I did not come close and I did not lower them. I said, "I just can't do this, I'm going to cover them with earth, but I can't lower them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this, did your medical condition deteriorate even further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the time when I entered the camp, when I saw that this was meant for Muslims, my health condition kept deteriorating. It was beyond what I could take, I was, when I saw dead bodies I was shocked and I could not even think about what to do health wise. I couldn't help myself, and I was walking around like a robot or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this we were taken to Busovaca near the mosque, and they assigned two guards and ordered us to walk through Busovaca to look for the dead and wounded, and we were to do that exclusively in Bosniak houses. The guards which escorted me kept warning me to walk slowly. However, I had such a buzz in my ears, I was in such pain, and I was in such a state that I did not hear this. At one point one of the guards cursed me and told me that he would shoot me in the back. Given my state, I turned around and I told him to just shoot, "I'm dying here every second, shoot me if you feel like it." Then they ordered us, in cases where the houses were locked, to break in and to search the houses. I searched four houses, I did not break in anywhere; but inside I could notice that somebody had been there before, because the more valuable things were missing, such as appliances, those things had been looted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this we were taken back to the camp, and in the evening we were ordered to again board a vehicle. In fact, at first they took us to different cells so we were not together. In the evening we were called out again and we were taken to a place called The Blue 11, which was owned by Katava Blazan. They ordered us to dismount, they told us to go through a gauntlet. I don't know if they were in uniforms or in civilian clothes; but as I passed through the gauntlet I thought this was, that these were soldiers, because I was struck by a hard object which I construed to be a rifle butt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Blue 11, this was a restaurant; was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a long time it was a restaurant, yes. For a while it was also a store, but for the most part it was a restaurant or a cafe type place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that went with you that night when you were called out that night, were they the same people that had been called out during the day, or were they different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same people. These were the same people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went through this gauntlet, how many, approximately how many people were standing on either side of the gauntlet that you had to go through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dark, there was no electricity, and we had to cross maybe 30, 50 metres in order to enter the structure. I don't know how many people were there, but we all received, we were all hit as we were passing that distance. Different people received a different number of blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you as you went through the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They cursed us. In my statement I deliberately did not emphasise what they were saying, but it was balija's mother. It was sort of ethnically based. But this was something that was done throughout my stay. The curses were just a part and parcel of it, so, I'm not specifically pointing it out. It was something that was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you entered the restaurant, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were ordered to sit down on the floor. There was no electricity, there was no light of any kind, and then several men appeared, two, three, I don't know how many, and they sort of shined their flashlights at our faces and then when they -- and he said out loud, "Oh, just take him out to the bridge, slit their throats and let them be taken down river." Then later on the same thing happened, another one showed up, shone his flashlight on our faces and he said, "I don't know what to do. The best thing would be to just kill them, put them in the oven so that they are all burned, and if you don't want to, take them to be human shields." Then they left. Then we stayed there sitting, I don't know how long. Another man walked in, he had a stocking mask on, and started singing songs which were traditional Bosnian songs. Then at one point he asked us, "Is there a Hodza or a Haji among us?" We kept silent. He repeated the question. He had asked this question twice before. He said, how many "aets" were there? How many sections were there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Hodza, that's a religious person isn't, it a muslim religious person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the men who lead the religious ceremony and Hoji is a person who had visited Mecca and Medina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked how many sections the Koran had. I said, "Listen, I don't know there are any people who know these things." I think that he didn't like having been recognised by me under this stocking mask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You call him by a nickname, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It just came out, I did not mean to. It just came out. That was not my intention for me to let him know that I had recognised him. It just came out because we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his face disguised in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a stocking mask over his face and he had a knit cap with slits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the topics which he entertained in his conversation. Because I knew that he was involved in this. That he was studying these Islamic customs and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you mentioned his nickname, what did he do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said, you, the smart one, if you know the answer to this question, I am going to have the last word. He meant he would have the last word. And he asked me, did I know what the word "hedija" meant, hedija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Knowing that this is a Turkish word and it means "gift" I told him that it meant gift. And he said, well, I am giving you your lives as a gift. Then he walked out. He walked out of the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we were taken back to the vehicle. The same procedure followed. I was lucky that with the exception of a few slaps I did not receive any hard blows. In the vehicle I was ordered to lower my head and not to look around. I heard screams, moans of others who were boarding the bus. I know that one man sustained serious bodily injuries there. I am not going to mention his name here, but it was a Bosniak man who, if he wishes, I think has an opportunity if he so desires to come here and testify himself before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now were you then taken back to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken back to Kaonik. In the morning again, and this may have been a different composition of the group, but most of the members of that group were taken to the village of Kula, and we were ordered to go to the frontlines; of course, escorted by the guards, of whom certain guards were wearing masks and the others did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the guards armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were called out that morning, were you told where you were going and what was going to happen before you were taken to Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I need to point out here that this was steady practice. There was a whole system going. That the people who were in the camp were assigned to digging trenches and making fortifications for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that you were taken to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because I know this terrain. I even own some land where I was. I had a piece of property there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your medical condition like this next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was getting worse and worse. I was hungry and scared and I had stomach, abdominal pains, but I didn't think about it any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the Kula trenches, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw armed soldiers in an area. I saw artillery in placements. I don't know what these were, whether they were guns or mortars. I don't know, this was near the property of Alija Zulum. Then, from there, we were taken to the frontlines. You could see the BH army lines not farther than 500 metres from there, and I was ordered to dig a trench which was completely open in an area which was not sheltered and a guard who guarded me was behind cover. However, I have to say that he was very fair and that he told me not to raise my head very much. He was talking to me more as a person than ordering me. But he made me dig. I had to dig, even though I told him that I was not well and he said, I'm sorry, but I was ordered to make you dig and you have to finish this work. Somebody was bringing water and I asked for some and then when I tasted it, I realised that it was creek water. I asked to be taken to the spring, which was between the two lines of defence. I not allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was it day or night when you were digging in the trench?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is daytime, yes, it was still daytime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you only taken trench digging once or did it happen on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you. That day we dug and at dusk we were taken to a house and placed in a room where we were told that we should get some rest. This could have been eleven or twelve at night because on that day, that very same day, an HVO soldier took away my watch, which was a souvenir. I know who this person is, but I am not going to mention his name. So we were in this house and someone I believe found a canned goulash or something. It was beef goulash, it was small, 100, 150 grams and we found a piece of stale bread in a window. I think that mice had already got to it. We split it evenly among all of us. In the morning, we were taken to dig again. I went back to finish off a part further down, which was a safer place. You could see the army, BH army soldiers walking about. Nobody shot. Later on I learned that the army knew that these were Bosniaks and that they were under orders not to shoot. They knew that these were the Busovaca Muslims and the HVO used this to fortify their lines. Later on the other events followed. However, on that particular day, we dug there and, meanwhile, a commander appeared on the scene. This guard had told him that I asked to go to the source. I did not hear him say this, but he was pointing in this direction, so I concluded from it that this is what he was telling him about. Later on we were taken back. This was on the second day in the evening, we had dug for a day, and then a night, and then another day. Then on the evening of that second day of digging, we were taken back there and we spent a night in the cells, again separate, always with different men. There I learned that this was done towards Rovna and Tisovac, that some people were badly injured. I saw people in passing who had their heads or arms bandaged with bruises. This was just in passing as we were passing each other in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that were injured, did you believe them to be injured as a consequence of going trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, beaten up physically. It wasn't firearms or anything. I don't know of any such occurrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time of your trench digging were you allowed to have rests and breaks during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you're talking about organised breaks for the entire group, there was something like that. I already told you that they would take us for a bit of rest. But if you're talking about me, personally, this guard did not force me to work beyond my ability. He realised that I was sick and he said, well, dig because this has to be finished. But he said, you know, do bit of digging and get a bit of rest, so it was really a human touch. He cared about me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of anybody in your group being beaten or mistreated during the time that you were trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area was wider there. I mean the lines were wider. I already mentioned that I knew that a person had sustained serious injuries. But I think that he can testify before the Tribunal himself, so I don't think I should take up more of my time by describing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened after you'd been taken trench digging? Were you subsequently released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, after all these events at Kula, the trench digging there and after returning to the prison, I was ordered to move to another hangar, which was next to this official part. There were about 150 people in this other hangar. We did not go out to work. We could relieve yourselves inside in the hangar. We had a wooden pallet and a blanket respectively and we stayed there until the end, until the 8th of February. To the best of my recollection, the representatives of the International Red Cross did not come there. The conditions were impossible, but since one did not have to fear for one's life and being killed, then it was bearable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever seek permission to go and see the doctor again after your initial visit to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after everything that had happened it didn't occur to me. To tell you the truth, I was afraid of repression. I was afraid of being sent to an even worse place where they beat people up even more, like Rovna, Pisovac so I didn't even think of doing it. So I didn't even ask for anything more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 8th of February, it was said that there would be an exchange, or rather, that we would be released. We were offered the possibility of leaving, going back to our homes, all of us, back to Busovaca, or rather, who wanted to could go to Kacuni, or rather, Zenica. At that point in time, the representative of the International Red Cross, I think his name was Mr. Gianni Lucca (check), said that the HVO authorities guaranteed the safety of all who would go back to Busovaca. Buses were lined up and people hurried towards these buses. Again, at this hangar, I mean above this hangar, Gianni Lucca stood up there, people were already moving toward the buses, and it just so happened that I was lingering on, and he said that at the very last moment that he found out from the representatives of the authorities in Busovaca that they could not guarantee the safety of Bosniaks in Busovaca. I entered the bus to Zenica and I abandoned my original intention of going back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you wish to put questions to the witness? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Witness V. I am Attorney Mikulicic and I am Defence counsel in these proceedings. I am going to put a few questions to you and I kindly ask you to kindly answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. V, you said in your introduction you did your military service in the former JNA, and that after serving in the JNA you were not involved in the reserve corps of the JNA; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was not in the reserve, I mean, formerly I did not go out for military exercises, but I did have work duty assignments. I was not in touch with weapons, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, if I understood you correctly, after returning from the former Yugoslav People's Army, you did not have any obligations involving weapons, but you were given work assignment duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, tell us, since you had this kind of assignment, were you included in certain records? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I imagine that I was registered with the military authorities, the secretariat of defence as a military-aged man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. V, did you ever, upon returning from the JNA and until these war events that occurred in Bosnian Herzegovina, did you have any kind of duty assignment that you carried out as part of this assignment of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really, except for planning total national defence and social self-protection. I already mentioned that, but I didn't have any major duties to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us briefly go back to mid-1992, approximately. My colleague, the Prosecutor, asked you something about this, so I shall have a few questions in this regard as well. Do you remember, Mr. V, whether Busovaca was attacked by the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember there was shelling for one day by aircraft sometime in the evening. That is when the old municipality building was set on fire and also a shop of Tisovica. I personally took part in extinguishing the fire together with Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the aircraft of the former JNA shelled Busovaca, there was some damage on the territory of Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this fire, were some buildings destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They burned down these buildings. I don't know whether they actually collapsed, but I know that some buildings burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. You also mentioned that together with the other people, you participated in alleviating this damage, could you explain exactly what you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was spontaneous, so that the fire wouldn't spread to the department stores, so we brought in fire hoses and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you did, was that part of the work duty you had or was it done in a different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't really an organised fire extinguishing activity. The firemen came from Zenica only later. It wasn't any kind of planned activity. It was sort of a civic activity. I just happened to be there and tried to help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. V, did you ever, before these events, at the beginning of 1993, have an opportunity of visiting Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You mean the camp?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the facility, the Kaonik facility. Do you know what was there in that part of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just knew that it was a warehouse of the former JNA, but I had no opportunity of visiting it. I passed it on the road, like everyone else, but I didn't really have any opportunity of going there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it true that you did not know what was in those buildings that you could see from the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you could not see these buildings from the road, I never saw them from the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. V, you mentioned a few times that you had certain health problems, could you tell us from when have you had these health problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but I think I had an ulcer for about ten years or so. I discovered it, I don't know, five or six years ago or something, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned on a few occasions that one of the consequences of your health problems was a certain psychological condition, were some of your problems due to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally. As we usually say, I mean, we, the ordinary people, we say that this is a question of nerves, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take any medicine for that? Did you receive treatment for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there is no efficient medicine for this. It is only natural that I took care of my own lifestyle. I tried not to get upset, and I tried to consume the kind of food that would not upset me, but I was not a 100 per cent disciplined patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a smoker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, you mentioned the events from the end of January, 1993, when you were taken to the Kaonik facility, do you remember what preceded this event when you were taken away to Kaonik? Was there some shooting? Were there any incidents of this nature? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that some of these Bosniak facilities were destroyed a few days before that. But I did not have an opportunity of hearing this shooting. I mean, as I was leaving the building I could hear shooting, but I didn't know where it came from. This is when I was being taken out of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. V, that you heard some artillery fire from the surrounding hills around Busovaca, did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did understand me correctly. This was May or June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was mid-1992, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this at the time when the JNA attacked Busovaca by aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, this was after that. This is when the Bosniaks were not allowed to put on the municipality building the flag of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, so this was mid-1992. Mr. V, you said you lived in an apartment building with 32 apartments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that on the morning you were taken away, you were the only Bosniak Muslim in that part of the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that, floor, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. V, where were the other Bosniak Muslims at that time, the people who otherwise lived in this building, how come you were the only one to be taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How should I know? These are neighbours and everyone has movements of his own. I know that I was the only person from that floor who was in the camp and I didn't see anyone of my neighbours there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on did you perhaps hear what happened to them, where had they gone, where did they disappear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not disappear. A lady, who was my neighbour with two children, she was in Kacuni, same with her sister. A Bosniak had rented his apartment to a Croat at the beginning of 1992, and at the beginning of 1992 this Croat moved in, so this man never came again. So, the impression was there were a lot of Bosniaks, but there were basically only three of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, Mr. V, your family, were they with you in the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had a daughter who lived in a Serbian flat in Busovaca, together with a roommate who was a Croat girl. There was a crisis at that time in Busovaca, and before these shops would be blown up in Busovaca she went and took some food to this daughter of ours, and it wasn't really advisable to move around a lot at that time. In the meantime she spent the night there because there weren't any buses, as this was otherwise, so this was irregular, and she stayed on. From my Croat neighbours I phoned her, because when those businesses were blown up our phones had been disconnected, and I asked her, and she said, "Why don't you send a car to pick me up?" I didn't have a car and I didn't ask any taxi drivers because nobody would drive, And I said, "Well, I'll see." So, it just so happened that I couldn't go to Zenica and she couldn't come back, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your wife had gone with your daughter to Zenica before these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, what I was trying to say was she took food to our daughter in Zenica, and she had a Croat girl, a flat mate, in a Serbian owned flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far back was that compared to the day were you taken in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of that was taking place during the same week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. V, what happened to the wives of your other neighbours who were Bosniak Muslims from this apartment building? Did they stay on in this apartment building, or did they go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only Bosniaks, not only wives, some Bosniaks stayed in the apartment building and some of them sooner or later moved out of Busovaca during 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I was not very clear, but I'm asking you about these events at the beginning of 1993, when your wife left, when she went to take food to Zenica. What then happened to your other lady neighbours who lived in the building there? The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there, most of them were there. I'm not aware of individual cases, but most Bosniaks were living in Busovaca at that time. They lived in fear, but they did go on living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, let us go back to the morning when you say that three men came to pick you up. Were they civilians or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore camouflaged uniforms and they were not civilians, they wore camouflaged uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to see some insignia, perhaps, on these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, you probably know that in 1992 all kinds of insignias and uniforms had gone through Busovaca, and I didn't really pay much attention to this, there were all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after that you were loaded on a bus and taken to Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you arrived in Kaonik, did somebody receive you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, we were just taken to the cell and three men walked in, two had stocking masks and one had revealed his face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. V, the guard from the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore camouflaged uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't watching, but they had standard insignia. No, I mean, I simply didn't pay attention to this, because one knows what it could have been. I mean, simply, I didn't look. So, if I saw a checkerboard, I wouldn't look at the letters that were inscribed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally think that these people were in Kaonik as guards? Were they members of a military unit, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
