utterances.text: I think they were, because they were workers of the railways who got jobs in this prison. I think they had some kind of assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. But, generally speaking, I think they were members of the HVO. This is my personal opinion. Whether they had anything special in there, I don't know, because I'm not aware of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You mentioned after that, that the next day your name was called out and you were sent to the cemetery in Busovaca. Tell me, Mr. V, -- oh, yes, and you also mentioned you were escorted by guards -- tell me, Mr. V, at the cemetery in Busovaca, as you were working there, were you escorted and guarded by those guards who were in Kaonik, otherwise, in the prison? Or were these a different set of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer with certainty because of my fear and because of my physical condition. I really wasn't paying any attention. But judging by their behaviour and the further contacts we had, I mean, you know, the people I could see, that it wasn't those guards. I'm trying to say this about the people I knew personally to be guards. I don't think that they were really escorting me. I think they were different people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps recall, regarding the people who were escorting you to work, were they also members of the army, members of a particular unit; or can you not recall this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the army, they were a member of the HVO, they were wearing camouflaged uniforms, weapons, they were real soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, you also stated that you were taken to Kula. Were you there guarded by the guards from Kaonik, or by some other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that the guards whom I knew at the Kaonik camp, those who were working inside the camp, I did not see outside. They never escorted me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, it's clear to me. I wasn't sure whether it referred to Kula. You also mentioned in your testimony that on one occasion you were taken to the restaurant called the Blue 11, which used to be, which was a restaurant; do you know, at the time when you were brought there, what the purpose of that facility was? Was it still a restaurant, or was it, did it have any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was exclusively used by the HVO. I don't know about the entire period, but it was exclusively for the HVO. With the exception of some stoves, nothing could show you that this was anything that would serve as a restaurant. I knew that only that I would be sleeping there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a person whom you recognised and that you addressed this person by his nickname. Do you happen to know his full first and last name, in addition to his nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I would prefer not to say that. I think I provided a full picture and I believe this person is dead. My information is that he may have been killed by the HVO. I don't know why. I don't know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you do not wish to reveal the identity of this person, but let me rephrase the question. Mr. V, does the person of whom we are talking have anything to do with Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he does not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, do you know, given that you know who this person is, whether this person had any mental problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible, that is entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us any further information on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that -- INTERPRETER: Excuse me, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, sorry for interrupting, but I think that the answer of the witness was not well heard by the interpreters; so, could you repeat your question and the witness will repeat his answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your interjection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, perhaps we're talking too fast and the interpreters did not manage to interpret this last exchange. So, let me repeat the question. My question to you was: Do you know anything regarding the person whom you did not want to identify, and who talked to you at the Blue 11 facility? Did this person have any mental problems? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe -- you see, I'm not a doctor, so I'm not able to evaluate a mental condition of a person. I know that from time to time this person was prone to drinking, but I also knew that this person did some creative work, as well. He was an intelligent person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you knew that this person had some alcoholic tendencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know this, but occasionally he would drink. Then, again, I cannot explain really how he ended up there at that particular time, if he was an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, in your testimony you mentioned that on the next day, in the morning, your name was called out; is that correct? When you were taken to work in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who called you out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not see this, because the guard was standing in the hallway and calling names out loud. So I could not see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. Do you know whether you were called out by the guard who was guarding you inside the prison, or was it someone who was escorting you out to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see who it was out there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned your visit to the physician in Busovaca, in the health centre. You mentioned that on that occasion you received an injection and some pills; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Kaonik, could you take medication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were offered to me, a guard would offer them to me, like, he said, "Pick one." I did not know what they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, do you recall, when you came back from the initial visit to the physician in Busovaca, where were you taken; back to the same building from which you had started out or to another one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the guard brought you to a table and that you were about three metres away from that table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe where this table was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the middle of the hangar, sort of like in front there. It was like this (indicating). It's hard for me to recall all the details, but I think it was somehow in the middle of the hangar, sort of off to the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say in the middle of the hangar, can you say, was this the same building, the same hangar where you were put in the cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's the same hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it was the same hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any electric power there in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, you mentioned that a man was there at that time whom you construed to be the warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what everybody was calling him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall how I was dressed at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wearing military or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how this person looked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was shortish. I saw him more from the back than looking at him in the face. He was in a hurry. He seemed in a hurry. He seemed to avoid me. He was a shortish man, definitely younger than I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known this person before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that during your stay in Busovaca, even though you were not particularly active in politics, you said that you still attended certain meetings in the municipal structures in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was up until 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Was that prior to the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, you said that in the building where you were staying a TV crew showed up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They invited everybody who wanted to pray to go and pray, and after that nobody from my cell was ever offered this. Later on I learned that on television they said that all the prison inmates were allowed to do their daily prayers, and so on. Now I can say this only about the cells where I was. I wasn't, I didn't have the full picture of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who these people were, this TV crew who came there? Were they foreigners or Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not Bosniaks, they were not foreigners. I cannot say who they were, but I know they were not Bosniaks, because that was not possible at that particular point in time. This is what I conclude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that later on you heard that this footage which was taped in Kaonik was later broadcast in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that from the people who had remained in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What programme was it? What television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, I was in the camp at that time, I could not follow those. I just heard that it was broadcast on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who saw it on television did not tell you on which programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not go into it. I just heard it in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, did you also take an opportunity to offer prayers at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. My mental condition was such, and the conditions for this has to also be special ones concerning the personal hygiene and everything, I was not able to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, you mentioned your work in the cemetery and later on in Kula, in the trenches. On those occasions was anybody injured or wounded among your group who worked there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except for the incident at the Blue 11, there was nothing. I saw some people farther down that were digging there. I saw some of them being bandaged, I don't know what type of injuries they sustained. I heard some had been beaten, they were hit with pickaxes and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you personally did not see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, you mentioned that when you dug trenches at Kula you were also guarded and you mentioned a guard who was watching, who was guarding you, and who had a humane, who treated you humanely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in comparison to the others, and from what I have heard, I think that I was lucky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know, was this a member of a military unit, or was it one of the guards from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, he was not from Kaonik, he was a member of some military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. V, during your stay in Kaonik, were you personally beaten by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that on 8 February you were released, that you left Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that you went to Zenica on a bus and that is where your family was already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family was in three different parts of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After coming to Zenica, did you visit --?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your arrival in Zenica, you said you visited a physician?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your complaints at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same ones which I had, bleeding, and my being undernourished, it sort of peaked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of therapy were you given at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was pretty much the standard therapy. I don't think that it differed much from the one which I was getting in Busovaca. Maybe I received different types of pills, different brand, but the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days did you stay in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't wish to really answer that, but it's somewhere in the range of 15 to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Neimann, any further questions you wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness V, I have a number of questions that I wish to put to you. If I understood you well, you told us that in Busovaca you had seen a number of soldiers bearing a number of different insignias and with different uniforms. Have I understood you right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you understood it correctly. During 1992 in Busovaca it was like a fashion show of uniforms and insignia. There were the HOS units, the Croatian Council, that is how we were calling them; however, it turned out it was the Croatian army. There was the HVO, there was the Black Shirts, a group would pass and they also had some U signs there and parading with weapons. They were always there. There would always be some passing around, so it was a process of militarisation, if you will. They did not harm anyone, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question: You also said that it was very unusual that people from the Kaonik camp go to dig trenches, that's what you said, that it was not usual for them to go and dig trenches. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that it was normal, but it did work, that is a fact, the whole camp was on the move, as it were. Because there were frontlines and we had 15 days to reinforce those lines. So it wasn't a normal thing, we had to do it, we only had 15 days for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see. Did you see other people who were not detainees from the Kaonik camp digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see it, because at the time, when I was in the camp, Bosniaks could not move about. I could not see anyone except in passing, one or two elderly persons. But Bosniaks did not have freedom of movement at the time. They could not go out, and I did not see any other persons digging except the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But do you know if other people were asked to go and dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I believe that in the period while we were in the camp that only prisoners were taken to dig, but I cannot say whether a labour unit was also established or formed in the town. That I cannot speak to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You also told us about your return from the medical centre in Busovaca. You told us that when you returned to the camp, after the visit, you had found a person standing in the middle of the hangar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One person in the middle of the hangar. When we came back from the health centre the guard told me to wait at a distance, which was at least three metres, and then he approached a person and turned this paper over to this person. I did not hear them, but given the gesture, it was like this, I thought nothing doing, they have to go to work. That is my understanding of what the gesture meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But I think I heard you say that you thought it was the warden standing in the middle of the hangar. According to you this person was the warden of the camp, and the reason you thought this was that the other people were addressing him in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it was the warden, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So right now you've just recognised and identified Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski. Can you say again that this person was Zlatko Aleksovski, was it him that was standing in the middle of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I could see here, I did not want to ask that he get up and take off his headphones. I recognised him by his face, by his eyes. I don't know if I made a mistake, but I believe that I did not. I did not request for him to get up to turn around. I did not look him in the eyes, so to speak, his face, but I think I remember him quite well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So you're not 100 per cent sure that this person who was standing in the middle of the hangar was, in fact, Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Yes, that was the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. Witness V, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for coming here to testify before the International Tribunal. We wish you a safe journey home. Thank you again, you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could now take another break before letting the other witness come in. We shall now take a 20 minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If, Your Honours, please. Might I call the next witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Niemann, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I call the next witness, Witness W, if Your Honours, please. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, can you hear me? Please stand up. Please remain standing, sir. Thank you. You will now take the oath. The usher is holding out the text for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please read the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may now be seated. Do you feel comfortable, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. To begin with you will answer the questions put to you by Mr. Niemann, the gentleman on your right. Mr. Niemann, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Niemann:

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, Your Honours have granted in your favour certain protective measures. First of all, we will refer to you as Witness W during the course of your testimony, and the image of your face is being distorted so it can't be recognised. I would like you, please, to look at a piece of paper I am now going to show you. I don't want you to read out what you see on the paper, but can you tell me whether the name that appears on that piece of paper is your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please, I ask that it be tendered under seal. May it be given the next exhibit number in order?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit No. 138.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness W, can you tell their honours what year you were born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Directly? Should I say this directly? Will this be heard?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us the year, you don't have to tell us the month and day, just tell us the year you were born.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Forty-six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What municipality were you born in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: May I say that? Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What education did you receive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 8th grade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't receive any secondary education?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live in Busovaca all the time from right up until 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I lived in Busovaca from 1980 onwards. I was in Germany for ten years and three months, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any military service during the time that you lived in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. I left on the 22nd of 1965 and I came back in 1967.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the military service that you did the traditional conscription service that every citizen had to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It was regular army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you do this military service for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Eighteen months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any special training other than the standard military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I was a cook in this army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had finished military service, did you then continue to have contacts with the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I was a plain worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992/'93, were you in any way involved with the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I mean -- do you mean when I was in Busovaca? Is that what you're saying? No, I was not duty-bound to any army in Busovaca because Busovaca was occupied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom was Busovaca occupied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: HVO. The defence council of HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: In '93, on the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the 25th of January, 1993, were you, yourself, in any way involved in political matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the work that you did from 1980 up to 1990/'91 of a civilian type of work, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I worked at the steel works until 1991 or 1992. I can't remember the month exactly because, you know, I had to wait for a certain period of time. I mean, I am still waiting until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "wait," what do you mean wait, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I mean I don't have a job. I am unemployed. That is what waiting is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what were relations like between Muslim people and Croat people in the Municipality of Busovaca prior to January 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, you know, 1991 and 1992, these relations were good. All of a sudden this Croatian army began to gather there and the Muslims were not allowed to walk around. They didn't dare walk around and stuff like that. You know, because it was occupied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Croatian army you're talking about, was that an army from Croatia itself or are you talking about a Bosnian Croat army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Bosnian Croats are concerned, well, there were quite a few people from elsewhere, you know, from Herzegovina. They didn't wear masks on their eyes, whereas the local people wore masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that how you're able to distinguish between locals and people who were foreign to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, those who didn't have masks I could not recognise. I had never seen them anywhere, but the men with masks, of course, you cannot recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people that weren't wearing masks, were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, camouflage uniforms they wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any badges or any insignia on their uniform that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I don't know HV, HVO, that I could notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw both HV and HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did conditions between the Muslim people and the Croat people in Busovaca deteriorate towards the end of 1992 and in the early part of '93?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, from 1992 it had already started. I mean from the beginning of January they started getting together. Then there were barricades. There were very few Muslims. They had already started fleeing from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any particular incidents that you saw that were directed against Muslim people in Busovaca at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I can only tell you the truth, what I saw with my very own eyes when I was supposed to be imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when were you -- were you arrested in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I was, on the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell Their Honours about how it is that you come to be arrested on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: On the 24th I was at home. I noticed from the window of my home, on the windows that were on other buildings near the roof I saw rifles, and I realised that these were snipers. I was afraid to stay at home with my wife, so I withdrew to Kadica Strana to Alija Arnaut, to his summer kitchen. There were many women, children, us civilians. The siren went off twelve times in the morning. That was an alert to the best of my understanding, and then they started shooting. There was a lot of shooting from the hills. Above my head I saw a few houses on fire. Then, we threw out white sheets as if we were surrendering ourselves because there was a lot of explosions there and what have you. A colleague of mine left the house. He took a few steps and he was wounded. We could not walk up to him to give him first aid. We threw a rope to him so that he could tie himself with that rope, and that we could drag him back to the door. That is where we gave him first aid. Then orders came from above, from the centre, I mean the Carsija downtown. We were supposed to follow the women and children and our hands were to be tied and we were supposed to look straight ahead of us. As we left in the direction of the centre, I saw on the bridge a man called Ceri. I don't know his real name, they always called him Ceri. There he laid dead on the corner of the bridge. On the road leading to the Carsija, to downtown, as we reached town, one of the HVO people in camouflage uniform said -- he shouted, rather, all of these guys should be shot. They started shooting bursts of gun fire, but above our heads. Then they said, you should separate yourselves from the women and children. That's what we did. A bus came and took us to Kaonik, to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stopping you there for a moment. Now you said that when you were walking to the house to take shelter, you saw snipers. Do you know what army or organisation these snipers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I figure it was the HVO because quite a few Muslim people had left there, so it was probably them, I reckon. And I am claiming that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that were firing on the house that you were taking shelter in, did you have any idea of what organisation they belonged to or connected to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I figure it was the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the orders for you to come to the centre, who gave those orders? Who was responsible for giving those orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the orders came from town, from the Carsija, from the HVO. The town was full of them, and I am sure that they were the ones who ordered this. Because there was no other army, except for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were put on the bus and you were taken to Kaonik, what happened when you arrived at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: When we arrived at Kaonik, they put us in a hangar. That is where the People's Army of Yugoslavia was before. So it was an empty hangar and we were ordered to walk against the wall. That we were supposed to be facing the wall and that we should keep our hands up also on the wall. I understood those orders well. Zlatko ordered that four rifles were to be cocked and a guard came. He searched all of us. He went from one man to another. I saw a neighbour of mine, he was so frightened that he collapsed. He was standing at my left. Perhaps he thought that they would shoot, so he fell. He collapsed. When all of this was over, we turned towards them, facing them, and then cigarettes, lighters, money, depending on who had what, we were all supposed to put that in one place, in one place. Then I think on the left-hand side, they put people who had diabetes. These people were supposed to say that they had diabetes and they were sent home. But I had thrombosis in my left leg and I have thrombosis until this very day but I stayed on. I spent the night there. I lay on a pallet. Together with a colleague, we had to share one single blanket. There was no light. There were only candles. We got soup there, some kind of tea and I don't know what all. Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that Zlatko ordered the four rifles were to be cocked. Who are you referring to when you say "Zlatko"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: The one who was the commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you known him before you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that he was the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I knew when I was transferred from this hangar to the cells, when I was taken to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come on to that in a moment. Now, you say that some people were separated; did you say anything about your medical condition at all when people were being asked about their medical conditions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: "I have thrombosis and my leg hurts, may I go home?" And he said, "You cannot go back."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you say this to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: This guard that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you spend in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Two days, I couldn't take it any longer because my leg had flared up, it was swollen because of the cold, you know. My legs were shaking, and I was shaking, and I went to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it come to pass that you went to see a doctor? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I reported to the guards, and they wrote down that I could go see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recognize any of the guards that you approached about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I did. His name is Ivo, and his nickname is Keba. I don't know his last name, but we called him Keba, everybody always called him Keba, all the people who worked with me at the steelworks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to him about your leg, your condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Because he was aware of my health condition from before, I was, had this flare-up before, so, I was walking on crutches, and he knew that I had that and he was helping. I have to say, I don't want to say anything against him, he was good to me, and he helped me go to Busovaca to the health centre. I was received there, but these physicians were not known to me. I could not see the ones whom I had known from Busovaca, so, these were unknown to me. But they received me, they gave me medication and such. The lady physician gave me a document so that I could have therapy at home, so that I would not go back to the cell, because she had examined my leg. But when I returned, a person called Marko drove me there, and two guards I did not know. So, I arrived at the hangar, and as you enter the hangar, to the right there was an office, this was Zlatko's office, and I told him I was told to go home and get therapy there. Then he said, "Take him to cell 12, it's warmer there." So that's where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Zlatko did, and that's when I met him well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him on other occasions, Zlatko, on other occasions when you were in the camp from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see people from time to time address him as the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I did not, because the cells were locked. Only if you needed to go to the lavatory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that you would be able to recognize him again if you saw him now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: You mean now? Oh, yes, I think I could recognize him right away, I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look around the courtroom and see if you can see the person whom you spoke to when you came back from the doctor? Just look around, and if you can, can you point to him with your finger? Just look around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Very well, yes. All right. I will start from this side. May I get up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: He is down there next to the policeman. He's sitting on this side, to the right of the policeman. If it's not enough, I can point him with my hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I think just for clarity you might point with your hand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: (Indicating). It's the person over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the witness has identified the accused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the piece of paper that was given to you by the doctor, did you read that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I did not read it. My eyesight was weakened, and without glasses I could not read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave this piece of paper to Mr. Aleksovski, did he appear to read it, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: He just glanced at the paper a moment, and then he ordered the guards to take me to cell 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the piece of paper then? Did he give it back to you, or did he keep it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: He kept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then? What was the next thing that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: That was in the cell. Later on I was taken to Kula to dig. There was a vehicle called a Rab, and several of us boarded it, and this Rab was taking people back and forth. There was some gravel in it, too. As we were taken in the direction of Kula, as we were going up that road, he was driving very fast, maybe 100 an hour, and then he would brake very suddenly, and then we would collide, we would bump into each other and we would roll over, and we would get all bruised and bloody from this gravel, and in such a shape we arrived there to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who called you out to go trench digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: The guards. It was the guards who were calling people out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people, approximately, were called out for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I cannot recall, a hundred, maybe even two hundred, depending on the need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're talking about the total number over the whole time. How many people were called out in the time that you were put in your truck and taken to Kula; can your remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I cannot recall, because the hallway was full, it may have been up to 100 people there. It would be split up into two, three groups, or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you told what was going to happen? Did they tell you in advance where you were going and what you were going to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that took you, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, they were, they were armed with rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you think might happen to you if you tried to escape or get away from these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: We were told right away that if we attempted to escape, that we would be shot on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken to Kula, what happened when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: When we arrived there we would, they indicated how many metres of trenches we were to dig and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where you were working in relation to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: This was at Kula, this was in the direction of the village of Solokovici. That was in that area, this line of, the HVO line of defence was in that area, and I spent two or three days there digging. I observed that people were making our people take off winter coats and leather jackets. Also, they made them take off jewellery, rings, and I also noticed that people were beaten. That was further down. I was in the upper part of this line, there was no beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How close were you to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to their lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. You mean what the distance was between the two lines? That I don't know. I don't know if I can recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the opposing lines of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from where you were trench digging?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I did not. No, there was a forest over there, so, you could not observe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you under guard when you were building these trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. They were about one or two metres away from us, at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards, were they taking shelter at the time that you were digging the trenches, or were they standing out in the open?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: They stood nearby, and sometimes they would take shelter behind a tree or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it daytime that you had to dig trenches, or was it only in the nighttime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I dug both during daytime and later into the night. Sometimes very, very late, until 8 or 9 o'clock, and it was very dark by that time because it was winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your leg still sore and giving you trouble at the time that you had to dig these trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, and even to date I feel it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to take breaks when you needed to, from digging the trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: When digging trenches? No, there were no breaks. You had to dig until you were done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long a stretch, in number of hours, approximately, did you have to continue digging? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Five or six hours, perhaps, and then you would rest. Otherwise, the men over there would say, "Dig, or else," and then you knew you had to dig.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given food and water during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did. It would be one can of fish for every two persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go trench digging on just the one occasion, or was there more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I spent three days at Kula, and after that I never went there again. I noticed the people were being beaten there, and I was afraid. Also, I noticed that people were bloody, that they were swollen, and I said, "Why, what is this?" And they said, "They are beating us." And I pretended that my leg was even in worse shape just so that I could get out of this situation, which was hell like for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from being taken to Kula for trench digging, were you taken anywhere else during the time you were in the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not have a watch and I could not follow the time. I don't recall when it was that they took us to a cafe called the Blue 11. We were taken there in that same Rab vehicle which used to take us to Kula. The order was given that whoever was to peek out from this vehicle would have their head chopped off. There was a vehicle going in front and one behind it. At that time I was talking to a colleague, and we said maybe we should just say good-bye now because we both thought we would be killed. When we arrived at this 11 Blue place, which I had not known until then. "Fuck your balija mothers," that's what they met us with. "Now you will see who we are." And we just kept quiet. We were sitting in this Rab vehicle, and the order came, "Jump out now," and we all jumped off from this Rab to the ground with our hands up. Then they said, "Cross your fingers up there." I had a hat on my head. There was a gauntlet, there were two cordons, one to the left and one to the right. I don't know what they had on them, some clubs or bars, and the moment I started walking I received a blow over my head. As we were entering the Blue 11 to the right, behind the bar, I saw camouflage uniforms and masks over their faces, and sharp knives. We passed by and there were some benches over there on the other side. We sat down with our heads bowed and they said, "Whose throat are we going to slit first?" I felt like my bones were melting from fear. We kept silent. In the end I recognised Ivo Popovic, called Isus. He had a hat on his head, he came over and he said, "God be with you." We kept silent. He said, "Good evening." We kept silent, "Selam Alejkum," we kept silent because we didn't know what to expect anymore. He said, "You are not, the benches are not for you to sit on. You should sit down on the floor." I didn't know what to do. I didn't know. Then he started talking to us and I asked him, "Ivo, can I light a cigarette?" "Yes, you can." Then he said, "Why don't we light a candle for, a Holy Mother's candle, it will be their last one." So, there was one man who was sharpening the knife over in the corner, and he said, "Who are we going to kill first?" I was smoking a cigarette. I think I smoked it in two or three long drags. And he said, "We should make a mop to mop the floor with his stomach." Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you might go a little bit slower so the interpreters can follow you. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you, I will slow down. So, we kept sitting there and talking, and he kept talking to a colleague of his, and he said, "You know, I'm supposed to slit your throat. Or maybe I should do this, I should do that." I kept thinking. Then, when the candle was finished, and then he said, "Let's light this Holy Mother's candle." And they did, and we were waiting to see what was going to happen next. Then one of them said, "First we will shatter their knees with bursts of fire and then we will slit their throats." So, it went on like this. Nobody had any watches left, we used to have them, but they were all taken away. Then a bus arrived, and I heard that the elderly people from the village of Ocenici arrived, and we were over there. I heard him again say, "Fuck your balija mothers. Eat of that calendar with (inaudible)." That was Ibrahim Nuhagic. They all joined us there when we came out and the bus came to collect us. When we boarded the bus, as we were boarding one by one with our heads bowed, you could not look left or right, Fehim Mujkic was boarding. His nickname was Borovo, because he had a store of the Bata shoes; so, they used to call him Borovo, because it was the same company. He had a store there, and he had an employee there, and this is whom I noticed from this corner of my eye, because I could not really look openly, and he stopped him by pulling him by the shoulder. Then I saw how he was kicked and beaten with the rifle butt. In the end I asked him, "So, how could you get up so fast?" He said, "I had to get up, because if I stayed down too long, they will just bash me in." So, they beat him for a long time while the bus was standing there. Then later when he finally got on, I saw him all bloody and moaning. In the back of the bus there was somebody in a camouflage uniform and a rifle and a mask with the slits. I recall well, when he boarded the bus he had an M-48 rifle, when he was passing the driver and a neighbour of mine, Hamdija Lusija was his name, he hit Hamdija over the head. I thought he would just go and fall unconscious. He said, "Where is Osman, your brother? Because I'm going to get him." Hamdija said, "I don't know." And he said, "Yes, you do." He left, and he said, "I don't know," and he said, "Don't talk to me like that." So Hamdija stopped talking. So, we arrived at the MUP building in Busovaca, and one of them said, "What are we going to do to these pigs?" That's what I heard him say. And he said, "Take them to Kaonik." And we were taken to Kaonik to the cells. When we arrived there, it must have been 12 or 1 o'clock, they kept beating us until about 5 in the morning. I remember very well when Senad Lusija was called out, Senad, yes. He immediately started screaming. Certain Kermo, yes, Biogradlija were called out, and this beating continued on from midnight or 1 until 5. People were bloody. I could not take that any more. So I knocked on the door, because I was very upset. I had four boxes of pills and I said, I am going the finish this. I can't take this any more. A colleague, Nasim Kemis said you'll survive this, don't do it. So I listened to him and I decided not to. So I got out on to the hallway and I went to the lavatory and there I found Mr. Ivo Keba, a guard, and I said, "Kabo, what is going on here?" I am not going to say any names. They said their own names. These were all snipers in Busovaca, so they are being beaten. I am thinking to myself, how are they -- what snipers? There was not a single army soldier in Busovaca, they couldn't have been there. Can we take a break now, I would like to relax a little bit, if I can?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure, you can have a drink of water, if you feel that would help.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Very well. I have a little bit of a headache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think we can finish up very quickly. Unless Your Honours propose to have a break now. We can finish fairly quickly. Were you then subsequently released from the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I was released on the 8th of February to the best of my recollection because, when the Red Cross came, some people went to Zenica, some people went to Kacuni and I don't know what all. I was talking to my neighbours and they said, will you go home? I said, yes, I will. Because all of these disasters were over and I wanted to go to my home, I didn't want to be a refugee. As I boarded the bus, I saw that there weren't very many of our people on the bus and I came back home. I was very dirty. I hadn't been shaving for quite some time. I was scabby and I wanted to take a bath. My wife said look, look, at all of this, look at all these problems. I said, "What kind of problems?" She said, "We have to run away." I said, "What do you mean?" She said, "People are coming all the time and saying that we should leave." She said that three men came while I was in the camp and when they came to my place, they took my wife upstairs to an attic. I mean, there were two rooms up there and some kind of kitchen, or rather, it is the attic of my house that is empty. There are two rooms in the kitchen; downstairs there is nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually have to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We shall now take a break to allow the witness to rest and relax a little bit. After that, we will have cross-examination by Mr. Mikulicic. Just a second, please. So we will take a fifteen minute break. That will leave us an hour and maybe we'll be able to get to finish this testimony by the end of the day. I don't know whether there is going to be anything tomorrow. Well, we don't know either. It's difficult for us to tell you anything about what's going to happen tomorrow. We will do our best. We will try to ensure that you won't have to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If we take a fifteen minute break, we'll have an hour left and maybe during this hour we'll be able to finish your testimony, sir, but I can't guarantee that. Fifteen minute break.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: All right, all right thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic -- excuse me, may the witness be brought in, please. (The witness entered the courtroom) Witness W, do you feel at ease? Are you ready to go on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So you will now answer the questions put to you by the Defence counsel, Mr. Joka. Mr. Joka is the gentleman on your left. Mr. Joka, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Joka:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall be putting a few questions to you with regard to the statement you made today. So let us take the same order that you took when making your presentation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, tell me, after your doing your military service in the JNA, were you in the military records in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No. When I came back from the JNA, I went to Germany in 1970 and I was there until 1982. I was temporarily employed in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then upon your return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Upon my return I came back on the 14th of March, 1984. And I was employed in the steel works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have military assignment in the steel works?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have any military assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any civilian assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have work duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No, I was a plain worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us now move on to the statement you made.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that down in Busovaca at some point in time one could see other armies too, that there was HVO and quite a few people from Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you tell that they are from Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I didn't know those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know them and therefore --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could they have been Slovenians, you didn't know Slovenians either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where Herzegovina is? Is it Bosnia or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, it is related to Bosnia, you know, as Bosnia-Herzegovina together. Because one says Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on specifically to this 24th of January, 1993, when you were actually taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that actually a day earlier you had been watching neighbouring windows from your own house. If I understood you correctly, in these neighbouring apartments, it was Muslims who lived there otherwise, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: There were very few Muslims in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the building across the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were there any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: They had left. They left earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They left earlier. You said you saw some kind of rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I saw rifles up in the attic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was standing behind these rifles? Do you know or are you just assuming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I figure they were HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court what to "figure" means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think. You're guessing, assuming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or did you see it with your very own eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I saw rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you see men behind those rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, you cannot see them when they are behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us after that that you hid with -- that you took shelter at Kadica Strana with women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the orders then came, if I heard you correctly, orders from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Women and children can go ahead and the men with their hands up in the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: As we were staying in this house, there was a lot of shooting going on, a lot of bullets flew across us. I saw women fainting and children --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I am asking you something different. You said orders came, how did these orders come in? Did a messenger come in and bring them? A soldier? A courier? How?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: We threw out those white sheets, you know, as if we were surrendering --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you told us that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how did the orders come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: From down there in the centre, they called. And who came? I don't know. I mean that we should surrender, and that we should move in the direction of this street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, so you don't know. You said that in town in the Carsija, a soldier of the HVO shot above your head and said that you should be separated from the women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that he was an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Because he had insignia, I saw it up there, he had a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then you also said that you were taken to Kaonik on a bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody escort you on that bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, there was one in the front and one in the back with rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, with rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. A couple of observations. First of all, you must slow down. Think of yourself; think of the witness. You need to wait after each intervention. I can see from my seat that the interpreters have some problems following. Second observation, Mr. Joka, you can use a microphone on your right, maybe it would be easier for you. Is it possible to change microphones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The reason I ask is that it would be much easier for you to use a microphone on your right. It's the microphone that is meant for this particular usage. You know, it's just a technical question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I have taken note of your comment as far as the speed is concerned. But it is easier this way, by the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We came to my question, who escorted you on this bus? You told us that there were two men with rifles, and now I am asking you whether they were civilians with guns or soldiers with guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: They were soldiers. They had camouflage uniform on them, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, certainly they were HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you were driven to the hangar --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I quote, "Zlatko ordered to have four rifles cocked?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that it was Zlatko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Because I heard one of them say Mr. Zlatko. I understood him well when he said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: One of the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What gentleman was he referring to, Mr. Who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, he was certainly referring to the commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know he was referring to the commander of the camp and not some other Zlatko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I claimed it was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you found out only later who the warden was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: When I went down to the cells, that is when I became fully aware of the fact that this was this Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it is only later that you realised that Zlatko was the warden, but this very first day when you arrived, you could not have known that Zlatko was the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't have. Because -- I mean, I could because I understood him to say, Mr. Zlatko, Mr. Zlatko, so that was it. You know, stand along the wall. Because we had our lives at stake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to remember the name of Zlatko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Teloslovski (as pronounced).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have my front teeth and I can't pronounce it properly. I cannot enunciate clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well tell us how you can tell it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I haven't got these teeth. Teloslovski (as pronounced).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, since when have you had thrombosis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I had thrombosis some ten years or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive regular treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you were taken to a doctor in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An unknown doctor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people who took you there, were they soldiers of the HVO or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: They were soldiers of the HVO, guards. Guards of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify matters further, as you were coming back, you said there were two soldiers too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I imagine those were the same two men, HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I know, I know, that there was one who was called Marco, but I don't know his surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they HVO soldiers, that's what I am asking you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you were taken to dig at Kula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you there, civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that at the location where you were digging you were being guarded by guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these guards from Kaonik or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: They were soldiers in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that from digging you were taken back to Kaonik, escorted by armed men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that you were taken to a facility which is called Jadanplaz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken by civilians or rather driven by civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: It was a civilian vehicle, Rab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but who escorted you, who went with you, soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I can't tell because it was nighttime and there was a vehicle behind us and a vehicle in front of us, and we were up there, closed up in that box, you know in the Rab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were there at that facility, were they civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Soldiers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Soldiers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a certain Ivo Popovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Called Isus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that man from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him before too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court whether this man was "normal," as we customarily say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I didn't understand you, I mean what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people consider Ivo Popovic, called Isus, a normal person or an abnormal person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I figured he was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said what was going on at this facility called the Blue 11, and then when you came to the MUP in town, that in the MUP they told them to take you back to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave these orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: A guy from MUP, he walked out because we weren't allowed to watch, we were just supposed to look straight ahead and I heard him say this from the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are now going back to the beginning. When you were brought there, you said that all your personal belongings were taken away from you, and that over there at the hangar you were supposed to hand in your cigarettes, lighters, whatever you had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you mentioned also to us that when you were at the facility called the Blue 11, that you lit a cigarette?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I asked Mr. Isus, Mr. Ivo and he allowed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, he gave us some, but some of us had cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that at one point in time, you decided to take four boxes of tablets, of pills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get these pills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I got them from the lady doctor when I went to see her at Busovaca at the outpatient clinic, the first time I went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take medication unhindered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, she gave he these pills and she told me to take them, according to a certain schedule, you know, three times during one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, what do you do for a living now? Do you have a farm? What do you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I am a refugee now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you became a refugee, did you have any land of your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Yes, I did have some land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your introduction that you were employed at the steel works, but that you were waiting. Then, when my learned colleague of the Prosecution asked you about this, he said -- you explained to him that you were jobless.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, I am jobless until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to give a full explanation, does that mean that you do not have a job or are you on welfare or did you have welfare, social security, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, you know, we were getting these packages with oil, flour, et cetera, from the steel works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, as you were waiting, I am asking you whether you till your land?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, look, you have to do it, you have to live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you manage to do that because you're ill, you have this sick leg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well, you know, my brothers would come and they'd help me out and I could work as long as I could work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one could work up to a point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Well you have to work, you have to live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, does the name Ivan Brnada?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Ivan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ivan Brnada?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I can't remember this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is supposed to be from the village of Putis. Allegedly you were neighbours for a certain period of time after you were released from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Oh, Brnada. No, I don't know that person. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Husnija Neslanovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: Husnija Neslanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If counsel wishes to ask about place names, that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Joka, you've understood what Mr. Neimann has just said, you know that this witness is a protected witness, and if certain names are said out loud it could have some detrimental effect on the witness, and on the protective measures that have been granted to him. So, if you need to give names of people, of places, we need to go into a private session, closed session. Do you wish to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly bear this in mind. I shall conclude my remarks by saying that I simply wanted to hear him say yes or no, whether he knew this person or not. This does not disclose the identity of the witness. Regardless of the answer I get from this witness, I shall have no further questions. So I'm simply asking him whether he knows a person by the name of Hvsnija Neslanovic, so that we would know for the continuation of these proceedings how to continue. I don't know this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a criminal record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my colleague tells me that the witness's answer has not been included in the transcript when he said "I do not know this man." It hasn't been entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, please repeat your question and the witness will repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I'm asking you, do you know Hvsnija Neslanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
utterances.text: I mean, there are quite a few people called Hvsnija, you know. But where does this Hvsnija work?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. You said that you do not have a criminal record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W
